speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the statement is the hon. gentleman's understanding of a certain condition, there would be no objection, but I always feel it my duty, where any apparent doubt is cast upon the honour of any member of this House, to call in question, as strictly as the rule will allow me, any such statement. The impression was somewhat given to me by the hon. gentleman's remark that some doubt Mr. CAMPBELL.
was cast upon the honour of a member of this House. I accept the hon. gentleman's statement as I understand him now to intimate that it was not intended to do that.

As I understand, he was calling in question the veracity of a statement of fact, and if he were in possession of information that justified him taking? that ground, it does seem to me that he should be at liberty to present the evidence which justifies the allegation. If he is in a position to do it, I think it would be quite right to allow him to do it.

I want to state to the House that ever since I have been in this House I have always-and I believe every hon. member must say the same thing- realized that the Deputy Speaker was making every effort to give us all fair play regardless of which side of the House we were on, and I am quite willing to bow at all times to his judgment in matters that appertain to the rules. There is one matter further to which I wish to refer, and I shall be very brief. We have vast expenditures being made on various public works. Well, there is one public work to which I wish to draw the attention of the government, and which I think would be of greater importance than any other they could undertake. I refer to the building of a canal system from Edmonton down the Saskatchewan river to its junction with Cedar lake at a place called Van Home, then cut across eight miles to Lake Winni-pegosis, thence down the Winnipegosis to Meadow Portage, a cut of one and a half miles, ten feet at the highest into Lake Manitoba, and from Lake Manitoba, a cut across into the Assinboine river. A canal of that kind with less than fifty miles of actual work and with less than ten wing dams on those various rivers would enable the people of Edmonton to ship their coal and. grain right into Winnipeg, the hub of Canada. A work of that kind would be surely far and away ahead of such a work as the Newmarket ditch, which is a ditch built where, I understand, there is no water, and where, if there was water, there are no boats; and where, if there were boats, there would be no freight; and where, if they could get freight, there is no place to take it. But if the government would build the canal I am asking them to undertake, that would be of real benefit to the people of the west and of all Canada and do something in the way of giving us an output for our traffic which would be exceedingly profitable. There is only one other remark I would make and that is with regard to the members from the west. I happen to be a Conservative and there are many who happen to be Liberals, but the interests of our people are the same, and I think the time has come when the men of the west, Liberals and

Tories, ought to get together and unite on any question of policy that will be of benefit to our people; and if they should do this, there are enough of them here to make any government sit up and listen and take notice.

I do not consider it necessary that I should at this stage of the debate take much time in replying to the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Campbell). I notice that he has thought it necessary to make one more reference to the fact that the right hon. the Prime Minister held for a certain time two seats in this House. That is a subject which seems to have caused a great deal of anxiety to hon. gentlemen opposite and given them the opportunity of ringing the changes on the outrage thus committed on the electorate. But, let me just point out that it was due to the course of action of parties, who were acting on behalf of the Conservative party, that the city of Ottawa was deprived of representation in this House the whole of last session. Hon. gentlemen opposite were within their rights in protesting that seat. The law allows that to be done, but the law was taken advantage of, not for the purpose of exposing corruption or unseating an hon. member, but for the sole purpose of working out some trifling party advantage. Hon. gentlemen opposite were not concerned at all about depriving the city of Ottawa of representation during a whole session, but solely with the view of acquiring some party advantage b^_keep-ing a protest, which was not intended to be acted upon, dangling over the head of the leader of the government. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) made a very strong reference to the premier of the province of Saskatchewan, and I regret verv much that he did not carry out his declared intention of waiting until the premier of that province had a seat in this House. The hon. gentleman referred to him as a traitor and a Judas, and I think it would have been more fitting to the credit and dignity of the hon. gentleman had he waited until Mr. Scott were actually present and could reply to any charge in person.
The hon. gentleman found a good deal of fault with my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) in connection _ with his stand on the question of the tariff. Well, I was anxious to learn what were the views of the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) on that same question. We have had a good deal of discussion on it from hon. gentlemen opposite, but not one of them has announced any policy whatever. It would have been interesting had the hon. member undertaken to tell us whether he was in favour of reducing the present tariff or whether he was in accord
with the majority on his side in advocating a general raise in the duties. But we have had no declaration of policy on his part, and in that respect he has followed closely in the footsteps of other hon. gentlemen opposite.	, ,	.	, .,
We have heard a great deal about the general extravagance of the government, but no attempt has been made to enter into any analysis of the increased expenditures of which these hon. gentlemen complain. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) started off with what no doubt was intended to be the main criticism of the government's management of our finances. In that criticism he made a general comparison of the expenses m 1896 with those of 1909. He chose a year in which there was very little capital expended by the Conservative administration and he bulked capital and ordinary expenditures together. He ignored the fact that since this government has taken office the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific has been entered upon, entailing the largest capital expenditure ever made in connection with any government railway. Adding the ordinary and capital expenditure of the two periods he made a comparison, and pointed out that in 1896, under the Conservative regime, some $42,000,000 were expended, whereas in 1909 the expenditure amounted to $133,000,000. But comparisons made in that way without any analysis are very misleading. What is necessary is to investigate these figures in detail If we confine ourselves, in the first place, to the ordinary expenditure m these two periods, then there was an expenditure in 1896 of $39,000,000 and m 1909 of about $84,000,000, but a very large part of the increase is entirely represented by cross entries. For instance, there is the running of the Intercolonial railway, the annual expense of running that road is part of the ordinary expenditure of the country according to our system of bookkeeping. You will find that the government expenditure on that Toad caused by adding new branches increased enormous-lv and forms part of the increased expenditure of which those hon. gentlemen complain. On the other hand, these expenditures are represented by an almost corresponding increase in the receipts of the road. Ihus, these figures represent merely cross entries. To make a fair comparison of expenditure we must deduct almost $5,000,000 from that item alone. The expenditure of the Post Office Department is another item standing on exactly the same footing. Then, there are the increased subsidies to the provinces-almost $5 000,000 of increased expenditures is represented by that item. If we take all the amounts from the public accounts which aTe mere cross entries of that kind, we

find that they male a total of about $19,000,000, and this sum must be substracted from the $84,000,000 in order to make a just comparison between the annual ordinary expenditures of the country in 1896 and in 1909. Even after that deduction is made there still remains a very considerable amount of increased expenditure to be accounted for. If hon. gentlemen opposite desired to draw any useful lessons, they would analyse that expenditure and point out to this side of the House the portions of it and the total amount that are unjust and unnecessary. Some items of expenditure have been increased enormously, and have been increased for the benefit of the country. Let me give one example. In the item of lighthouses and river lighting, during the last years of the Conservative regime, the total expenditure was less than half a million dollars, to-day it amounts to about two and a quarter millions. _ I contend that that is an increase that is entirely justified in the interests of the public. Our system of navigation has entirely changed since 1896. Deep waterways have been established from Dort Arthur to the ocean, harbour improve ments have been made and lighthouses have been established, all these things helping greatly to cheapen transportation it.1S., by fforng into_ items of that kind in detail that a true idea can be formed of the justification that exists for the increase in the ordinary public expenditure.

As 1 said, they select a year in which the capital expenditure was something between three and four millions of dollars and compare it with a year in which the greatest expenditure is made in the construction of the great National Transcontinental rail-[DOT]Wa7-i t*lese hon. gentlemen try to justify the comparison by saying that dur-me their regime they also constructed a great transcontinental railway. I take issue with them on that point. When they were in power and procured the construction of the Canadian Pacific, they did not procure the construction of a railway that belongs to Canada. The expenditure was handed over to a private corporation, and every dollar of money that was paid out of the public treasury, and every asset of the public that was turned over for the construction of that road, became the property of that private corporation. The road now being constructed and for which this government is now making capital expenditure is a road which, when comnleted. will belong to the people of Canada, a road for which a rental is to be paid beginning a short time after its -construction. So, there is no comparison between the expenditure on a transcontinental road made by the Conservative government and the ex- Mr. ROBERT SMITH
penditure on the National Transcontinental made by this government. Then it is contended, in comparing the debt incurred by the two governments, that it was made in the same relation, because the Transcontinental road was a part of the expenditure that went to increase the debt during the Conservative regime and the expenditure on the Transcontinental has caused the increase incurred- by this government. Again, I say the case is entirely different. The expenditure made by the Conservative government in connection with the Canadian Pacific railway is not all represented in the public accounts. A large portion of the expenditure made by Canada for the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway was not in cash, but in the form of lands and of road already constructed. This constructed road which was handed over to the Canadian Pacific railway company represented an ' expenditure of $30,000,000, which had been made prior to the accession of the Conservative government to power. These constructed lines are not represented by the increase of the debt made under the Conservative government, nor are the 25,000,000 acres of land-an asset of Canada-* which passed from being the property of the people to being the property of a private corporation. If this government had undertaken to build a transcontinental road under a similar bargain, they might have alienated the public lands and secured the construction of the Transcontinental road without the expenditure of a single dollar in cash out of the public treasury of Canada and without adding a single dollar to the debt of this country.
Now, I wish to say a few words in reference to the remarks of the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers). That hon. gentleman entered into a somewhat poetic representation of the actions of his party in connection with the government of this country, and took a somewhat poetic license with the facts. He contended that the Liberal party had opposed all the great measures put through by the Conservative party, and which, he claimed, had resulted in the present greatness of the country. He contended, in the first place, that the Liberal party of Canada had opposed confederation, and that Sir John Macdonald and his government' and party were the only ones responsible for that great Act and consequently for the greatness of Canada to-day. I think the hon. gentleman's memory is entirely at fault. As a matter of fact, Sir John Macdonald and the Conservative government, up to a very short time before the principle of confederation was adopted, had opnosed that principle against the Liberal party of this country, and it was only at the last moment that the Conservatives, joining with the Liberals, formed the coalition government to put through the measure. The hon. mem-
[DOT]2273

ber said that the Liberals had opposed the Canadian Pacific railway. I deny that; his memory is again at fault. Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, during the time he led the administration of this country, endeavoured to construct the whole of the Canadian Pacific railway by a bargain with a company on the basis of a land- grant. He failed to obtain favourable terms of that kind, and his government proceeded to construct that road as a government work, and, at the time Mr. Mackenzie left office, there had been an expenditure in actual construction of that road of no less a sum than $30,000,000. Yet hon. gentlemen opposite are, continually proclaiming throughout this country that Alexander Mackenzie and his party had opposed, tooth and nail, the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. The facts are that the Liberals in opposition opposed the particular terms of the bargain which was made by the Conservative government for the construction of that railway. They opposed for instance, the monopoly clauses, they opposed the clauses that allowed alternate sections of land to be laid aside and accumulate in value through the efforts of the settlers on the other sections. They opposed the exemption from taxation, and made other exceptions to the terms, hut it cannot be said that the Liberal party were opposed to the principle of constructing the Canadian Pacific railway, or that they ever intended to put any obstruction towards the accomplishment of that great work.
Now the hon. gentleman also thought it would be desirable that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) should hold some revival meetings for his side of the House; and shortly afterwards he gave us a very glowing account of the virtues and patriotism of the Japanese people. When he was waxing so eloquent concerning the virtues of these people, I thought perhaps it would be a good thing for him to hold a few revival meetings with the hon. members from British Columbia upon his side of the House. One would suppose that if these people possessed all the good qualities so eloquently described by the hon. gentleman his political friends would not have such a tremendous dread of rubbing up against the Japanese.
He also undertook to tell us that an immense amount of corruption had taken place since this government came into power, and he regretted very much that there seemed to be no virtue left outside of the Conservative party. I wondered if the hon. gentleman could not remember a few things that were not exactly virtuous on his own side of the House, in the midst of his own party. When he was going so deeply into Canadian history, he might have gone back for instance to the original bargain for the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway, which led to the great
Pacific scandal and the hurling of his party from power. If he had come down to later times, he would remember that it was this very corruption that was mainly responsible for the hurling of his party from power in 1896. Yet the hon. gentleman seemed to imagine that there was no virtue and no honesty outside of the Conservative party.
Now the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Boyce) had considerable to say in connection with the action of the Department of Militia and Defence in charging up to the town of Sault Ste. Marie the expenses of sending troops up there to quell dis-* turbances, or to maintain order. He had a strong opinion that the minister ought not to have rendered any bill for that service. Now, Sir, the Militia Act clearly defines what shall be done in such a case, the law is established by this parliament, and one would imagine that hon. gentlemen opposite would consider it to be the duty of any minister to fulfil the law, whatever it is, that he finds on the statute-book. Yet the hon. member for East Algoma makes it a subject of complaint that the Minister of Miiitia did not violate the law on this occasion, and that the town from which he hails did not have the advantage of that expenditure at the expense of the public treasury of Canada, without any authority of law. That hon. gentleman, and some others who have spoken, have taken a good deal of exception to what they call the fuss and feathers of the Militia Department. They have contrasted the total expenditure of the Militia Department in the latter years of Conservative rule with the total expenditure of to-day. Well, this is the first time I have heard that argument within this House. Upon the hustings this is a favourite theme with Conservative orators. I watched with some interest the submission of the militia estimates during the last session of this parliament, and I was astounded to find that, notwithstanding all the criticism of a general character that had been indulged in by hon. gentlemen opposite on various occasions, they allowed the estimates of the Militia Department to pass through this House practically without a dissenting voice. Now I claim that if these gentlemen, sitting on the other side of the House as guardians of the treasury, as they pretend, and knowing as they pretend to know, that there is absolute extravagance and waste in connection with these militia expenditures, it is surely a part of their duty as critics of the government to raise these objections when the estimates are being passed, if there are unnecessary officers in connection with the department, why is it that these hon. gentlemen, or some one of them, did not rise in their places and protest against the salaries or allowances for these unnecessary
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Ways and Means.

There are no resolutions to be proposed to the committee in view of the fact that there are no changes in the tariff; but it is the custom to keep the Bill in committee during the session. I will therefore move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
What effect will that have upon the subsequent proceedings? If it is called again next Monday the debate may go on.

It might, but the keeping of the Bill in the committee is pro forma entirely. The Finance Minister always wishes to keep the Bill of Ways and Means open during the session. That has always been the practice.
When may we expect the return ordered on December 6, showing the number of officials in Ottawa having living apartments supplied by the Crown?
I understand it will be laid on the table early next week.
